“Joseph! Joseph!” He then wagged his head and tapped upon it, indicating his opinion of Joseph's shortcomings.

“But, my dear young friend,” Mr. Pumblechook continued, “you must be famished; you must be quite worn out. Sit down. Here's a chicken brought over from the Boar, here's a tongue brought over from the Boar, and here are a few little extras from the Boar which I trust you won't scorn. Yet do I,” said Mr. Pumblechook, rising almost before he had settled into his chair, “behold before me the very one I used to play with in his happy infant days? And may I—may I—?”

By this May I he meant, might he shake my hand? I agreed; he shook it ardently, and resumed his seat.

“Here's wine,” said Mr. Pumblechook. “Let us drink our thanks to Fortune, and may she always choose her favourites so wisely! But still I cannot,” he added, standing once more, “look upon One—and drink the health of One—without again declaring—May I—may I—?”

I gave permission, and he shook my hand again, drained his glass, and inverted it. I followed his example; and had I stood upon my head before drinking, the wine could scarcely have reached it more directly.

Mr. Pumblechook served me the liver wing and the finest slice of tongue—no obscure pork cul-de-sacs on this occasion—and, by comparison, scarcely attended to himself. “Ah, poultry, poultry!” he exclaimed, addressing the bird on its dish. “Little did you suspect, when you was a fledgling, what awaited you. Little did you dream of providing refreshment under this lowly roof to one who—Call it weakness if you please,” said Mr. Pumblechook, getting up yet again, “but may I? May I—?”

It was becoming superfluous to repeat my assent, so he proceeded without it. How he managed this so often without injuring himself on my knife remains a mystery to me.

“And your sister,” he went on after eating steadily for a short time, “who enjoyed the honour of bringing you up by hand! What a melancholy picture, to consider that she can no longer properly comprehend that honour. May—”

Seeing another approach imminent, I checked him.

“We shall drink to her health,” I said.

“Ah!” cried Mr. Pumblechook, sinking back in his chair, positively limp with admiration. “That's how you can tell them, sir!” Who this Sir might have been I cannot say; it certainly wasn't me, and nobody else was there. “That's how you recognise a noble mind, sir!”

At the sight of these, Jupiter could hardly contain his delight, but his master's face showed profound disappointment. Even so, he urged us to keep working. He had scarcely spoken when I stumbled and pitched forward, catching the toe of my boot in a large iron ring half buried in the loose soil.

Now we worked with real determination, and I have never spent ten minutes in greater excitement. In that time we completely uncovered an oblong wooden chest. Its remarkable hardness and perfect state of preservation made it clear that the wood had undergone some mineral treatment, perhaps with mercuric chloride. The chest measured three and a half feet long, three feet wide, and two and a half feet deep. Riveted bands of wrought iron reinforced it, forming an open lattice around the whole box. Along each side near the top were three iron rings, six altogether, providing handholds for six people. Even with all of us pulling as hard as we could, we barely shifted it in the earth. We immediately realized we could not lift such a weight. Fortunately, only two sliding bolts secured the lid. Trembling and breathless with anticipation, we pulled them back. Suddenly an immeasurable treasure glittered before us. The lantern light fell into the pit and flashed back from a tangled pile of gold and jewels with a brilliance that dazzled our eyes.

I will not attempt to describe what I felt as I stared. Astonishment, of course, overwhelmed everything else. Legrand seemed drained by his excitement and said almost nothing. For several minutes Jupiter's face was as deathly pale as his dark skin could become. He looked dazed, thunderstruck. Then he dropped to his knees in the pit and plunged his bare arms elbow-deep into the gold. He left them there as though relishing a luxurious bath. At last, with a deep sigh, he exclaimed, apparently to himself:

“And all this comes from the gold bug! The pretty gold bug! The poor little gold bug I abused so cruelly! Aren't you ashamed of yourself, you black fool? Answer me that!”

Eventually I had to rouse both master and servant to the need to carry the treasure away. It was getting late, and we needed to make an effort if we were to bring everything safely indoors before daylight. Deciding how to proceed was difficult, and we spent a considerable time discussing it, since all three of us were too confused to think clearly.

One day, while occupied with Mr. Pocket and my books, I received a note through the post whose very envelope sent me into a flutter. Though the handwriting of the address was unfamiliar, I guessed at once whose it must be. There was no formal opening—Dear Mr. Pip, Dear Pip, Dear Sir, or Dear Anything—but simply these words:

“I am coming to London the day after tomorrow on the midday coach. I understand it was arranged that you would meet me? At any rate, Miss Havisham believes so, and I write in accordance with her understanding. She sends her regards.

“Yours, ESTELLA.”

Given sufficient time, I should likely have ordered several new suits for the occasion. As time was wanting, however, I had to make do with those I possessed. My appetite disappeared on the spot, and neither peace nor rest came to me until the appointed day. Nor did that day, when it came, supply either: I was worse than before, and began hovering about the coach-office in Wood Street, Cheapside, even before the coach had started from our town's Blue Boar. Perfectly aware of this though I was, I could not feel safe allowing the office out of my sight for more than five minutes together. In this irrational state I had completed the first half-hour of a vigil destined to last four or five hours when I encountered Wemmick.

“Hallo, Mr. Pip,” he said. “How are you? I should scarcely have expected this to be your usual haunt.”

I told him I awaited someone arriving by coach, and asked how the Castle and the Aged were.

“Both thriving, thank you,” replied Wemmick, “especially the Aged. He's in splendid spirits. Eighty-two on his next birthday. I've a mind to fire eighty-two rounds, provided the neighbours don't object and my cannon stands the strain. But this isn't London conversation. Where do you suppose I'm bound?”

“For the office?” I suggested, since he was heading that way.

“The next thing to it,” Wemmick answered. “I'm off to Newgate. We're engaged in a banker's-parcel affair just now. I've been down the road looking over the scene, and must consequently exchange a word or two with our client.”

“Was it your client who committed the robbery?” I asked.

“Bless your body and soul, certainly not,” returned Wemmick with great dryness. “But he stands accused of it. You or I might equally be accused. Either one of us might, you understand.”
